strings.name: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf
strings.role: Former Liberian president · Nobel Peace Prize laureate
strings.summary: Sirleaf moved from finance and international banking into politics, experiencing exile and imprisonment before winning Liberia’s 2005 presidential election. She became Africa’s first elected female head of state, led postwar reconstruction, promoted debt relief and women’s participation, and shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize. Her government also faced poverty, Ebola and criticism over corruption and appointments of relatives, exposing limits to its anticorruption achievements.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 13 November 2026. Selected milestones do not constitute an exhaustive record of all news or controversies.
strings.influence.rationale: Africa's first elected female head of state, she contributed to Liberia's postwar reconstruction and women's peace advocacy and received the Nobel Peace Prize.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: Harvard Kennedy School, Master in Public Administration (1971)
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Postwar democratic transition
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Led Liberia from 2006 to 2018 and transferred power to an elected successor at the end of her tenure.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Women and peace advocacy
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize with Leymah Gbowee and Tawakkol Karman.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Reflected on development and governance
strings.timeline.event-01.text: Called for transformative development at a governance symposium in Monrovia, where anticorruption remained a public concern.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Ended her presidency
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Transferred power to George Weah; her record combined reconstruction achievements with persistent corruption controversies.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Nepotism controversy
strings.timeline.event-03.text: Appointments of relatives to senior posts drew criticism from protesters and party members, challenging her reform pledges.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Shared the Nobel Peace Prize
strings.timeline.event-04.text: Recognized for women’s safety and participation in peacebuilding; won reelection in the same year.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Became Liberia’s president
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Took office after her 2005 victory, becoming Africa’s first elected female head of state.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Joined UN development leadership
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Led UNDP’s Regional Bureau for Africa before returning to Liberian politics.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Imprisoned under military rule
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Arrested after returning to Liberia for the election, experiencing political imprisonment and exile.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Became finance minister
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Joined William Tolbert’s cabinet before the following year’s coup disrupted her public career in Liberia.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Completed public administration studies
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Earned an MPA at Harvard after further studies in the United States.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Monrovia
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Born in Liberia’s capital and attended the College of West Africa.
